judgments.comparative_verdict: Both reports hit all five expectations with essentially equivalent substance and citations; Report 1 is marginally more thorough (e.g., notes the vacuous existing test and password rotation) but Report 2 is comparably rigorous with slightly clearer causal chain framing — overall comparable quality.

report_1.evidence: the migration only says ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; it never says ALTER TABLE appointments FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY... In Postgres, RLS policies do not apply to the table's owner unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is set. The deployment's runtime connection is now juniper_owner in every configuration surface — docker-compose.yml:5, infra/main.tf:2, and .env.example:1 all set DATABASE_URL=postgresql://juniper_owner:ownerpw@db:5432/juniper... Note this is *not* the superuser/BYPASSRLS variant of the bypass — the same comment states juniper_owner is an ordinary LOGIN role with neither attribute, the operative mechanism is purely table ownership + missing FORCE.

report_2.evidence: PostgreSQL exempts the table owner from row-level security unless the table also has FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY — ENABLE alone applies policies only to non-owner roles (superusers and BYPASSRLS roles are also always exempt, but db/migrations/0001_init.sql:1-3 explicitly states juniper_owner is an ordinary LOGIN role with neither attribute, so ownership is the exemption in play here)... docker-compose.yml:5, infra/main.tf:2, and .env.example:1 all set DATABASE_URL=postgresql://juniper_owner:ownerpw@db:5432/juniper.

report_1.evidence: It became exploitable on 2026-06-17, introduced by commit b2a23d2a527cd13589163a40ef51b2eb2a430af6 ("ROTA-214 run migrations from the api container on boot")... each changing postgresql://juniper_app:apppw@db:5432/juniper to postgresql://juniper_owner:ownerpw@db:5432/juniper: .env.example:1, docker-compose.yml:5, infra/main.tf:2

report_2.evidence: It became exploitable with commit b2a23d2 — "ROTA-214 run migrations from the api container on boot"... each flipping the runtime DSN from the restricted role to the owner role: .env.example:1... docker-compose.yml:5... infra/main.tf:2

report_1.evidence: Primary fix — restore the least-privilege runtime role. Change DATABASE_URL back to postgresql://juniper_app:...  in docker-compose.yml:5 and infra/main.tf:2... Defense in depth #1 — new migration db/migrations/0004_force_rls.sql: ALTER TABLE appointments FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

report_2.evidence: Immediate config fix (stops the leak): change DATABASE_URL back to postgresql://juniper_app:apppw@db:5432/juniper in docker-compose.yml:5 and infra/main.tf:2... Database hardening (fail-closed): add db/migrations/0004_force_rls.sql containing ALTER TABLE appointments FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

report_1.evidence: Defense in depth #2 — filter in application code. Add WHERE tenant_id = :tid (bound from claims["tenant_id"]) to the query in backend/app/routes/appointments.py:16-19, so isolation never depends on exactly one mechanism.

report_2.evidence: Belt-and-braces (optional but cheap): add an explicit WHERE tenant_id = :tenant_id (from the verified claims) to the query in backend/app/routes/appointments.py:16-19, so the app is not single-layered on RLS.

report_1.evidence: Boot-time assertion in backend/app/db.py (or an app startup hook): on startup, verify the connected role is not the tenant tables' owner and has neither rolsuper nor rolbypassrls (query pg_roles/pg_class), and that relrowsecurity/relforcerowsecurity are set on appointments; crash on violation rather than warn.

report_2.evidence: Refuse to boot when mis-wired. Add a startup guard in the backend: query pg_class/pg_tables and assert current_user is not the owner of any RLS-protected table (or assert relforcerowsecurity is true for appointments), and abort startup otherwise.
